trigger: Find two elements whose sum equals a target and return their indices in one pass.
key_idea: For each number, its needed partner is target minus itself; a hash map of seen values lets you check for that partner in O(1).
approach: Create empty map value to index
For each nums[i], compute complement = target - nums[i]
If complement in map, return [map[complement], i]
Otherwise store nums[i] -> i and continue
gotcha: Check for the complement before inserting the current number, or you may pair an element with itself.

trigger: Digits stored in reverse order in two linked lists and you must add them like grade-school addition.
key_idea: Walk both lists together, summing digit plus digit plus carry, emitting sum mod 10 and carrying sum div 10; a dummy head avoids special-casing the first node.
approach: Create dummy head and carry = 0
Loop while l1 or l2 or carry is nonzero
Take val from each list or 0 if exhausted
Append node with (sum % 10), set carry = sum // 10
Advance each list pointer if it exists
Return dummy.next
gotcha: Forgetting the final carry (e.g. 5 + 5 = 10) drops the last digit; loop must continue while carry is nonzero.

trigger: Longest contiguous substring satisfying a no-duplicates constraint.
key_idea: Grow a window with the right pointer and, on seeing a repeated char, jump the left pointer past that char's last index using a map of char to latest position.
approach: Keep map char -> last index and left = 0
For each right index, if s[r] seen at index >= left, set left = that index + 1
Update map[s[r]] = r
Update best with r - left + 1
gotcha: Only move left forward: a stale last-seen index smaller than left must be ignored, never used to move left backward.

trigger: Longest palindrome inside a string; palindromes are symmetric around a center.
key_idea: Every palindrome has a center (a char or a gap between chars); expand outward from all 2n-1 centers while characters match and keep the longest.
approach: For each index i, treat it as a center
Expand l=i, r=i for odd-length palindromes while s[l]==s[r]
Expand l=i, r=i+1 for even-length palindromes
Track the longest span found
Return that substring
gotcha: Forgetting the even-length center (between two chars) misses answers like 'bb'.

trigger: Digits stored in reverse order in two linked lists and you must add them like grade-school addition.
key_idea: Walk both lists together, summing digit plus digit plus carry, emitting sum mod 10 and carrying sum div 10; a dummy head avoids special-casing the first node.
approach: Create dummy head and carry = 0
Loop while l1 or l2 or carry is nonzero
Take val from each list or 0 if exhausted
Append node with (sum % 10), set carry = sum // 10
Advance each list pointer if it exists
Return dummy.next
gotcha: Forgetting the final carry (e.g. 5 + 5 = 10) drops the last digit; loop must continue while carry is nonzero.

trigger: Characters are placed in a visual up-and-down pattern across rows and read back row by row.
key_idea: You only need which row each char lands in, not the columns: walk a row index down then up, appending each char to its row's bucket, then concatenate rows.
approach: If numRows == 1 return s
Keep one string bucket per row and a direction flag
For each char, append to current row
Flip direction at row 0 and row numRows-1, then step
Join the row buckets in order
gotcha: numRows == 1 causes an infinite bounce or division by zero if not special-cased; the learner's matrix build is a heavier variant of the row-bucket idea.

trigger: Reverse the digits of a signed integer while respecting a 32-bit overflow limit.
key_idea: Peel digits with mod 10 and rebuild with rev*10 + digit, checking before each multiply whether rev would exceed 2^31 - 1 (or fall below -2^31).
approach: Record sign and work with abs(x)
Loop: digit = x % 10, x //= 10
Before rev = rev*10 + digit, check rev > (2^31-1)//10
Return 0 on overflow, else sign * rev
gotcha: The overflow check must happen before the multiply since the problem forbids 64-bit storage; also drop leading zeros from the reversed result like 1200 -> 21.

trigger: Choose two lines to maximize width times the shorter height.
key_idea: Start with the widest pair; moving the taller side can never help since the shorter one caps the area, so always move the shorter pointer inward.
approach: Set l = 0, r = n-1, best = 0
Compute area = (r-l) * min(height[l], height[r])
Update best
Move whichever pointer has the smaller height
Stop when l meets r
gotcha: Moving the taller pointer is the classic wrong move; the shorter side is the bottleneck.

trigger: Find all unique triplets summing to zero with no duplicate triplets in the output.
key_idea: Sort, fix the first element, then run two pointers on the remainder for a two-sum; sorting makes skipping duplicates a matter of comparing neighbors.
approach: Sort nums
For each i, break if nums[i] > 0; skip if same as nums[i-1]
Set l = i+1, r = n-1
If sum == 0 record, then advance both skipping duplicate values
If sum < 0 move l right, else move r left
gotcha: Duplicates must be skipped at both the i level and the l/r level after a match, otherwise repeated triplets appear.

trigger: Unique quadruplets summing to a target; a generalization of 3Sum with one more fixed index.
key_idea: Sort, fix two indices with nested loops (skipping duplicates), then two-pointer the rest for the remaining two-sum.
approach: Sort nums
Loop i, skip duplicates of nums[i-1]
Loop j > i, skip duplicates of nums[j-1] when j > i+1
Two pointers l = j+1, r = n-1 toward target
On match record and skip duplicate values on both sides
gotcha: Skip j duplicates only when j > i+1, otherwise you wrongly skip a valid nums[i] == nums[j] pair.

trigger: Remove a node counted from the END of a singly linked list in one pass.
key_idea: Advance a fast pointer n steps ahead, then move fast and slow together; when fast reaches the end, slow sits right before the node to delete.
approach: Create dummy pointing to head; slow = dummy, fast = head
Move fast forward n steps
Move both until fast is None
Set slow.next = slow.next.next
Return dummy.next
gotcha: Removing the head (n equals list length) breaks without a dummy node in front of the list.

trigger: Matching nested opening and closing brackets in correct order.
key_idea: Brackets close in last-opened-first-closed order, which is exactly a stack; each closer must match the top of the stack.
approach: Map each closer to its opener
Push openers onto a stack
On a closer, check stack nonempty and top matches, then pop
Otherwise return False
Return True only if stack is empty at end
gotcha: A leftover stack at the end means unclosed openers, so return len(stack) == 0, not just True.

trigger: Combine two already-sorted linked lists into one sorted list by splicing nodes.
key_idea: Repeatedly attach the smaller head to a tail pointer, like the merge step of merge sort; a dummy head keeps the code uniform.
approach: Create dummy node and tail pointer
While both lists nonempty, attach the smaller node and advance that list
Advance tail
Attach whatever list remains
Return dummy.next
gotcha: Forgetting to append the leftover tail of the longer list drops its remaining nodes.

trigger: Merge k sorted sequences into one sorted output.
key_idea: Keep one candidate per list in a min-heap so the next smallest element is always at the top; pop, append it, and push that list's next node.
approach: Push (val, list index, node) for each nonempty list head
Pop the min, append node to result tail
Push popped node's next if it exists
Repeat until heap empty
Return dummy.next
gotcha: The learner's code pushes every value into the heap (O(N log N) and rebuilds nodes); the optimal heap holds only k entries, and ties need an index tiebreaker since ListNodes are not comparable.

trigger: Rearrange adjacent nodes of a linked list without changing values.
key_idea: For each pair, rewire three pointers: prev -> second, second -> first, first -> next pair; a dummy node makes prev exist for the first pair.
approach: Create dummy pointing to head; prev = dummy
While prev.next and prev.next.next exist, name first and second
Set first.next = second.next, second.next = first, prev.next = second
Advance prev = first
Return dummy.next
gotcha: Save second.next before rewiring or the rest of the list is lost; odd-length lists leave the last node in place.

trigger: Reverse consecutive blocks of k nodes, leaving a short trailing block untouched.
key_idea: For each group, first confirm a k-th node exists, then reverse exactly that group in place and reconnect the previous group's tail to the new head.
approach: Create dummy; prevGroup = dummy
Find kth node from prevGroup; stop if missing
Set nextGroup = kth.next
Reverse nodes from prevGroup.next up to nextGroup, with prev starting as nextGroup
Link prevGroup.next to kth, set prevGroup to old group head
gotcha: Starting the reversal's prev at nextGroup (not None) automatically links the reversed block to the rest of the list.

trigger: Locate the first occurrence of a pattern string inside a text string.
key_idea: Slide a window of length len(needle) over haystack and compare each slice; KMP does the same in linear time but brute force is acceptable here.
approach: For i from 0 to len(haystack) - len(needle)
Compare haystack[i:i+len(needle)] with needle
Return i on the first match
Return -1 if none
gotcha: The loop bound must be len(haystack) - len(needle) + 1 or you miss a match ending at the last char.

trigger: Find substrings that are a permutation of a fixed set of equal-length words concatenated.
key_idea: Because all words have the same length, chop each candidate window into word-sized chunks and compare chunk counts to the required Counter, bailing early on any invalid or over-counted chunk.
approach: Build Counter of words; wlen, total = len(words) * wlen
For each start i up to len(s) - total
Scan chunks of wlen from i, counting into a seen map
Break if chunk unknown or count exceeds required
Record i when seen equals required Counter
gotcha: Words can repeat, so you need counts not a set; the optimal version slides per offset mod wlen to avoid restarting each window.

trigger: Sorted array that was rotated, and an O(log n) requirement.
key_idea: At any mid, at least one half is properly sorted; check whether target lies within that sorted half and discard the other.
approach: Binary search with low, high
If nums[mid] == target return mid
If nums[low] <= nums[mid], left half is sorted
If target in [nums[low], nums[mid]) go left, else go right
Otherwise right half is sorted; mirror the check
gotcha: Use >= when testing nums[mid] >= nums[low] so a two-element array counts the single-element left half as sorted.

trigger: Check no repeated digit within each row, column, and 3x3 box of a grid.
key_idea: Keep a set per row, per column, and per box keyed by (r//3, c//3); a digit is invalid if already present in any of the three.
approach: Create defaultdict(set) for rows, cols, boxes
Iterate every filled cell
If digit in rows[r], cols[c], or boxes[(r//3, c//3)] return False
Add digit to all three sets
Return True
gotcha: Box identity is integer division (r//3, c//3), not r%3; skip '.' cells so they are never treated as digits.

trigger: Fill a grid so that every placement satisfies constraints, with undo when a branch fails.
key_idea: Try digits 1-9 in each empty cell, recurse on the next cell, and undo the placement if the recursion fails; row, col, and box sets make validity checks O(1).
approach: Precompute row, col, box sets and list of empty cells
Recurse on empty cell index; index == len means solved
For each digit 1-9 that is valid, place it and add to sets
If recursion succeeds return True
Otherwise remove digit from sets and board, try next
gotcha: Forgetting to undo the sets when backtracking poisons later branches; also digits are strings on this board, not ints.

trigger: Enumerate all combinations that reach a target where elements may be reused unlimited times.
key_idea: DFS with a start index so combinations are built in nondecreasing candidate order (no duplicates), and recurse on the same index to allow reuse.
approach: dfs(i, path, total): if total == target record copy of path
For j from i to end, skip if total + candidates[j] > target
Append candidates[j], recurse dfs(j, ...) allowing reuse
Pop to backtrack
gotcha: Recurse with j (not j+1) to allow reuse, and never go back to earlier indices or you produce permutations of the same combination.

trigger: Minimum number of jumps to reach the end when each index gives a max jump length.
key_idea: Treat each jump as a BFS level: track the farthest reach from the current level and, when you exhaust the level's end, take one jump and extend the end to that farthest reach.
approach: Set curr_end = curr_far = jumps = 0
For i in range(n-1), update curr_far = max(curr_far, i + nums[i])
If i == curr_end, increment jumps and set curr_end = curr_far
Return jumps
gotcha: Loop only to n-2 (range(n-1)); including the last index would count an extra jump you never take.

trigger: Rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees in place without extra matrix.
key_idea: Either transpose then reverse each row, or rotate four cells at a time layer by layer using one temp variable.
approach: Transpose: swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for j > i
Reverse each row
Alternatively, for each layer l..r, cycle four cells top-left <- bottom-left <- bottom-right <- top-right
gotcha: Transpose then reverse rows gives clockwise; reversing columns instead gives counterclockwise, and in the layer method the offset i runs only r - l times.

trigger: Group strings that are rearrangements of each other.
key_idea: Anagrams share a canonical key; use a 26-letter count tuple (or sorted string) as the dictionary key and append words to that bucket.
approach: Create defaultdict(list)
For each word, build a 26-length count array
Use tuple(count) as key and append word
Return the dict values
gotcha: Lists are unhashable; convert the count array to a tuple before using it as a key.

trigger: Can you reach the last index given max jump lengths; asks feasibility, not count.
key_idea: Scan from the right keeping the leftmost index known to reach the end; an index i is good if i + nums[i] reaches that goal, and the answer is whether the goal becomes 0.
approach: Set goal = n-1
For i from n-1 down to 0, if i + nums[i] >= goal set goal = i
Return goal == 0
gotcha: A zero at some index is only a trap if nothing before it can jump past it; the memoized DFS the learner commented out is O(n^2) and can TLE.

trigger: Combine overlapping ranges into disjoint ranges.
key_idea: After sorting by start, an interval overlaps only with the last merged one, so either extend that end or start a new interval.
approach: Sort intervals by start
Push the first interval to result
For each next interval, if start <= last end, extend last end with max
Else append it
Return result
gotcha: Use max when extending the end; a later interval can be fully contained and have a smaller end.

trigger: Insert one interval into an already sorted, non-overlapping list and keep it merged.
key_idea: Three phases: copy intervals ending before the new one, merge all intervals that overlap it by min start and max end, then copy the rest.
approach: Append intervals whose end < newInterval start
While intervals start <= newInterval end, absorb by min start and max end
Append the merged newInterval
Append remaining intervals
gotcha: Overlap includes touching endpoints (shares a point), so use <= and >= in the comparisons.

trigger: Minimum cost path in a grid moving only right or down.
key_idea: The cheapest way to reach a cell is its value plus the cheaper of the cell above or the cell to the left; memoize by (row, col).
approach: Define dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1])
Initialize first row and column as running sums
Fill row by row
Return dp[m-1][n-1]
gotcha: Out-of-bounds neighbors must contribute infinity (not 0); the learner's top-down DFS can hit recursion limits on large grids so bottom-up is safer.

trigger: Find the largest integer whose square does not exceed x without using pow.
key_idea: mid*mid is monotonic in mid, so binary search on the answer range and keep the last mid whose square is <= x.
approach: Set low = 1, high = x//2 + 1
While low <= high, mid = (low+high)//2
If mid*mid > x, high = mid-1; if less, low = mid+1; else return mid
Return high
gotcha: When the loop ends, high (not low) is the floor; also handle x = 0 and x = 1 where high starts at 1.

trigger: Count the ways to reach step n taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
key_idea: Ways to reach step n equals ways to reach n-1 plus ways to reach n-2, which is Fibonacci; only two previous values need storing.
approach: If n <= 1 return 1
Keep a = ways(1) = 1, b = ways(2) = 2
For i from 3 to n, set a, b = b, a + b
Return b
gotcha: Naive recursion is exponential; also base cases are ways(1)=1 and ways(2)=2, not 0 and 1.

trigger: Canonicalize a Unix path handling '.', '..', and repeated slashes.
key_idea: Split on '/' and use a stack of directory names: '..' pops, '.' and empty tokens are ignored, anything else is pushed.
approach: Split path by '/'
For each token: if '..' pop if stack nonempty
Skip '' and '.'
Push any other token
Return '/' + '/'.join(stack)
gotcha: '...' is a valid directory name and must be pushed; '..' at root must not pop from an empty stack.

trigger: Smallest substring of s that contains all characters of t including duplicates.
key_idea: Expand right until the window satisfies t, then shrink left while it still satisfies; track a 'formed' count of characters meeting their required frequency to test satisfaction in O(1).
approach: Build need = Counter(t), required = number of distinct chars
Expand r, update window counts, increment formed when a char hits its need
While formed == required, record window if smaller
Shrink l, decrement counts, decrement formed if below need
Return best window
gotcha: Increment formed only when count == need exactly once, and decrement only when it drops below need, otherwise the counter drifts.

trigger: Find a word by walking adjacent grid cells without reusing a cell.
key_idea: DFS from every cell matching word[0], marking visited cells in place and restoring them on return so other paths can reuse them.
approach: For each cell, start dfs(i, j, 0)
In dfs: return True if index == len(word)
Return False if out of bounds or char mismatch
Mark cell with '#', recurse into 4 neighbors with index + 1
Restore the cell and return the result
gotcha: Restore board[i][j] after exploring (backtrack); the learner's code returns True before restoring, which is fine only because the search stops there.

trigger: Sorted linked list where equal values are adjacent and you must keep only one of each.
key_idea: Since duplicates are adjacent, compare each node with its next and skip over nodes with the same value by rewiring next.
approach: curr = head
While curr and curr.next exist
If curr.val == curr.next.val, set curr.next = curr.next.next
Else advance curr
Return head
gotcha: Do not advance curr after deleting; there may be a third duplicate right behind.

trigger: Largest rectangle under bars; each bar's rectangle extends until a shorter bar on each side.
key_idea: Keep a stack of increasing heights with their start indices; when a shorter bar arrives, pop taller bars and compute their area using current index as the right boundary, and the popped bar's start as the new bar's start.
approach: Iterate bars with a stack of (start index, height)
While top height > current, pop and compute height * (i - start)
Remember the last popped start as current bar's start
Push (start, current height)
Flush the stack at the end using n as right boundary
gotcha: Forgetting to drain the stack after the loop misses rectangles that extend to the right edge.

trigger: Reverse only a middle segment of a linked list between positions left and right.
key_idea: Walk to the node before left, reverse exactly right-left+1 nodes with the standard prev/curr loop, then stitch: pre-segment node -> new head, old segment head -> node after segment.
approach: Advance curr left-1 times, remembering prev as the pre-segment node
Save segment head = curr
Reverse right-left+1 nodes using prev/curr/temp
Connect pre-segment.next = prev (or head = prev if none)
Connect segment head.next = curr
gotcha: When left == 1 there is no pre-segment node, so the new head is prev; a dummy node avoids this branch.

trigger: Visit binary tree nodes in left, root, right order.
key_idea: Inorder is recursive: fully process the left subtree, record the node, then the right subtree; an explicit stack gives the same order iteratively.
approach: Define dfs(node): return if None
dfs(node.left)
Append node.val
dfs(node.right)
Return the result list
gotcha: For a BST, inorder yields sorted order; the iterative version must push all left children before popping.

trigger: Generate every structurally unique BST for values 1..n.
key_idea: Pick each value as root; all BSTs on the left range and right range combine independently, so the answer is the cartesian product of the two recursive lists.
approach: generate(lo, hi): return [None] if lo > hi
For each root in lo..hi, get leftTrees = generate(lo, root-1)
Get rightTrees = generate(root+1, hi)
Create a TreeNode for every (left, right) pair
Memoize by (lo, hi) and return the list
gotcha: Return [None] not [] for an empty range, otherwise the nested loop produces zero trees.

trigger: Is there any route between two vertices in an undirected graph given as an edge list.
key_idea: Build an adjacency list and explore from source with DFS/BFS using a visited set; reaching destination means a path exists.
approach: Build adjacency list adding both directions
Push source onto a stack, keep visited set
Pop node; return True if it is destination
Add unvisited neighbors to the stack
Return False when the stack empties
gotcha: Add edges in both directions since the graph is bidirectional; source == destination should return True immediately.

trigger: Count structurally unique BSTs on n nodes; only counts, not the trees themselves.
key_idea: With root i, the left subtree has i-1 nodes and the right has n-i, so count(n) = sum over i of count(i-1) * count(n-i), the Catalan recurrence.
approach: For nodes from 2 to n, sum dp[left] * dp[right] over every root choice
Store in dp[nodes]
Return dp[n]
gotcha: Only sizes matter, not actual values, so dp[0] must be 1 (the empty subtree counts as one way).

trigger: Check BST validity where every node in the left subtree must be less than the ancestor, not just the parent.
key_idea: Pass an allowed (lower, upper) range down the recursion: going left tightens upper to node.val, going right tightens lower to node.val.
approach: valid(node, lower, upper): return True if None
Return False unless lower < node.val < upper
Recurse left with (lower, node.val)
Recurse right with (node.val, upper)
Start with (-inf, +inf)
gotcha: Comparing only with the immediate parent misses violations deeper down; the bounds must be strict since equal values are invalid.

trigger: Compare two binary trees for identical structure and values.
key_idea: Two trees are the same if both are empty, or both nonempty with equal values and recursively same left and right subtrees.
approach: If both None return True
If exactly one None return False
If values differ return False
Return same(p.left, q.left) and same(p.right, q.right)
gotcha: Check the both-None case before accessing .val; the learner's threading variant adds overhead without changing complexity.

trigger: Check if a tree is a mirror of itself around the root.
key_idea: Compare two subtrees as mirrors: values equal, and left.left mirrors right.right while left.right mirrors right.left.
approach: Define mirror(a, b): True if both None, False if one None
Return False if a.val != b.val
Return mirror(a.left, b.right) and mirror(a.right, b.left)
Call mirror(root.left, root.right)
gotcha: Comparing left with left (same-tree style) is wrong; the inner children must be compared crosswise.

trigger: Return node values grouped level by level from a tree.
key_idea: BFS with a queue, processing all nodes currently in the queue as one level before their children are handled.
approach: If root is None return []
Put root in a deque
While queue nonempty, snapshot its length as the level size
Pop that many nodes, record values, push their children
Append the level list to result
gotcha: Capturing the level size before popping is what separates levels; the learner's approach queues whole level lists instead, which also works.

trigger: Level order traversal where alternating levels are read right to left.
key_idea: Do a normal level-order BFS and reverse every other level's value list with a toggling flag.
approach: BFS level by level as in level order
Collect values for the level
If zig flag is set, reverse the level list
Flip the flag after each level
gotcha: Reverse only the output values, not the child insertion order, or the next level's ordering breaks.

trigger: Number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path.
key_idea: Depth of a tree is 1 plus the larger depth of its two subtrees, with an empty tree having depth 0.
approach: If root is None return 0
Compute left = maxDepth(root.left)
Compute right = maxDepth(root.right)
Return 1 + max(left, right)
gotcha: Depth counts nodes not edges, so a single node has depth 1; iterative BFS/stack is safer for very deep skewed trees.
